name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,318

entries.clue: Demonstrate outside home about Northern Ireland? (8)

indicatorNotes.outside: the verb for demonstrate sits outside the rest, wrapping it
indicatorNotes.about: C (circa, Latin for around) is the standard abbreviation for about

blocks.note: to demonstrate a claim is to prove it

annotation.surface: A protester marches around outside a house, somehow concerning Northern Ireland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrate' tempts you towards a protest march, which the surface encourages. The question mark flags that Northern Ireland is one example of the answer, though it is often called simply 'the Province'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Northern Ireland is a region of the UK widely known as the Province.

entries.clue: Very good exercises for music-maker (4)

annotation.surface: A musician is praised for their practice routine.
annotation.walkthrough: PI (short for pious) is a crossword staple for 'very good' or 'holy'.
annotation.definitionFit: A pipe is a simple wind instrument, so it makes music.

entries.clue: Writer after short time turning up on American vehicle (7)

indicatorNotes.turning up: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters bottom to top, reversing them
indicatorNotes.after: the writer comes after the short time
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, the first piece sits on the next

blocks.note: the nib is the writing part of a pen

annotation.surface: An author, arriving shortly afterwards, climbs aboard an American vehicle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Writer' wants to be a person, an author; in crosswords it is as often the pen or its point.
annotation.definitionFit: An omnibus is the full, old name of the bus, a passenger vehicle.

entries.clue: I can run riot, somehow creating insurmountable barrier (4,7)

indicatorNotes.somehow: the letters come together in some unspecified order

annotation.surface: Someone boasts that their rampage will throw up an impassable wall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run riot' looks like the signal to rearrange, but those letters are fodder; the signal comes after the comma.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical name: the Iron Curtain was the Cold War division of Europe, a barrier people could not cross.

entries.clue: Yell having eaten that woman’s fruit (6)

indicatorNotes.having eaten: the yell takes the pronoun inside itself, as if swallowing it

annotation.surface: Someone shouts because a woman's fruit has been eaten.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the yell came because the fruit was eaten; in fact the yell does the eating.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain hypernym: the cherry is one kind of small stone fruit.

entries.clue: Some mouse droppings — not fresh (4)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters of the phrase are taken

blocks.note: the letters run from the third letter of mouse to the first of droppings

annotation.surface: Mouse droppings are found in the larder and they are not fresh.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap: mo(USE D)roppings. 'Some' reads as a quantity of droppings, not an instruction to take part of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: Something used is second-hand, no longer fresh or new.

entries.clue: Southern island’s device for diver (5)

blocks.note: Cuba is a Caribbean island; the 's links it to the definition

annotation.surface: A southern island is known for gear used by divers.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possession in the surface but works as 'is' in the cryptic reading: the island is the device.
annotation.definitionFit: Scuba is breathing apparatus that lets a diver stay underwater.

entries.clue: Old comedian Ken before start of day was unsteady (8)

blocks.note: Ken Dodd, a long-serving British comedian

annotation.surface: An elderly comic tottered about before the day began.
annotation.walkthrough: Ken Dodd was a British comedian famous for his wild hair and tickling stick, which is why 'Old comedian Ken' gives DODD.
annotation.definitionFit: To dodder is to move unsteadily, typically from age, so doddered means was unsteady.

entries.clue: Gasp needing oxygen in family show? (5)

indicatorNotes.needing: the gasp needs the gas placed after it to finish the word

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

annotation.surface: Someone gasping for air in the middle of a family show.
annotation.walkthrough: A panto (pantomime) is a British Christmas stage show for families, full of slapstick and audience shouting; the question mark flags the example.
annotation.definitionFit: Pantomime is the classic British family entertainment at Christmas.

entries.clue: Go into detail about former currency of UK (7)

annotation.surface: Someone explains the history of Britain's old money.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'former currency' as one idea, like the shilling; split it and the prefix joins money that is still current.
annotation.definitionFit: To expound a subject is to explain it at length, going into detail about it.

entries.clue: Favouring vivacity and speed, grow rapidly (11)

annotation.surface: Someone who likes liveliness and pace urges fast growth.
annotation.walkthrough: A straight three-part build; the comma is only there for the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cells or weeds that proliferate multiply fast, which is rapid growth.

entries.clue: Salt transported to Caribbean (11)

indicatorNotes.transported: the letters are carried off and set down in a new order

annotation.surface: A cargo of salt is shipped to the Caribbean.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like a link word joining 'transported' to its destination, but its letters are part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A bicarbonate is a salt of carbonic acid, as in sodium bicarbonate.

entries.clue: Expert countryman protecting cold bird (8)

indicatorNotes.protecting: the outer letters surround the cold letter, shielding it

blocks.note: a dab hand is an expert

annotation.surface: A skilled farmer shelters a bird from the cold.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Expert countryman' reads as one person; the expert and the countryman are separate pieces, with the cold letter protected between them.
annotation.definitionFit: The dabchick is another name for the little grebe, a small water bird.

entries.clue: Claim benefit around middle of March (6)

indicatorNotes.around: the benefit goes around the extra letter
indicatorNotes.middle of: take the central letter of March

annotation.surface: Someone applies for a welfare payment in mid-March.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Claim benefit' reads as one phrase about welfare; split it, and 'Claim' is the definition while 'benefit' is the container.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to claim something is so is to assert it.

entries.clue: Have a meal around six? Wonderful! (6)

indicatorNotes.around: around means surrounding here, so the meal word encloses the Roman numeral

blocks.note: to dine is to have a meal

annotation.surface: Someone is delighted at the idea of dinner at about six o'clock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Around six' pretends to be a rough time for dinner; it is an instruction to put the numeral inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Divine is used as an exclamation of delight, meaning wonderful.

entries.clue: Perhaps one or two, say, lodging in Bury (7)

indicatorNotes.lodging in: the abbreviation lodges inside the other word

annotation.surface: One or two lodgers are staying in Bury, a town in Lancashire.
annotation.walkthrough: Bury, capitalised, looks like the Lancashire town, but it is the verb. 'Perhaps' signals that one and two are examples.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one and two are whole numbers, that is integers.

entries.clue: Broadcast terrible news about leaders of the revolution (6)

indicatorNotes.terrible: the letters of news are made a terrible mess of
indicatorNotes.about: the rearranged letters go about the others
indicatorNotes.leaders of: take the first letters of the following words

annotation.surface: A radio bulletin announces terrible news of an uprising.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' pretends to be radio; its older sense is scattering seed by hand, and here it is a past participle.
annotation.definitionFit: Seed broadcast across a field is scattered widely, that is strewn.

entries.clue: Limited space in awful camp — torment (11)

indicatorNotes.awful: the letters are in an awful state, jumbled

annotation.surface: Prisoners are cramped in a dreadful camp and suffer.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash splits the fodder in the surface, but both words are rearranged together.
annotation.definitionFit: A compartment is a small separate section, a limited space.

entries.clue: Dance in the morning stopping unruly mob (5)

indicatorNotes.stopping: the time plugs the gap, stopping up the other word
indicatorNotes.unruly: the letters of mob will not keep their order

annotation.surface: Dancing early in the day halts a rioting crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unruly mob' reads as a set phrase; the adjective is the signal to rearrange the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain hypernym: the mambo is a Cuban ballroom dance.

entries.clue: Biblical children understand God ultimately (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: take the final letter of God

annotation.surface: Children in the Bible come to understand God in the end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Biblical' is fair because seed for descendants, as in 'the seed of Abraham', is mainly the language of the Bible.
annotation.definitionFit: In the Bible, seed means offspring or descendants.
annotation.definitionNote: SEED is a collective noun, matching the plural children.

entries.clue: Huge chaps crammed into tumbledown semi (7)

indicatorNotes.crammed into: the chaps are squeezed inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.tumbledown: the semi has collapsed, its letters rearranged

annotation.surface: Big men are squeezed into a rundown semi-detached house.
annotation.walkthrough: A semi is a British semi-detached house, one of a joined pair. 'Huge' reads as describing the chaps, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something immense is vast, huge.

entries.clue: Perspective of one of Germanic people coming to Britain (5)

annotation.definition2: one of Germanic people coming to Britain

blocks.note: a point of view on a subject

blocks.clueFragment: one of Germanic people coming to Britain
blocks.note: a member of the tribe that gave England its name

annotation.surface: A historian's viewpoint on the Germanic tribes who invaded Britain.
annotation.walkthrough: The Angles, with the Saxons, came to Britain in the fifth century; 'England' comes from their name.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a slant or viewpoint taken on a matter, and a member of the Angles, a Germanic tribe.

entries.clue: Experience negative vote being reported (4)

indicatorNotes.being reported: a report is spoken, so the word is heard, not seen

blocks.note: a no is a vote against

annotation.surface: A politician has experience of losing a vote, as the news reports.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Experience' looks like a noun, but it is the verb: to have known hardship is to have experienced it.
annotation.definitionFit: To know something, such as hardship, is to experience it.

entries.clue: Caused to be loved over grabbing attention (8)

indicatorNotes.grabbing: the word for over takes hold of the attention word, holding it inside

blocks.note: to give an ear is to pay attention

annotation.surface: Someone won affection by making a grab for attention.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Over' pretends to be a preposition; it means finished, as in 'the game is over'.
annotation.definitionFit: To endear someone is to make them loved, so endeared means caused to be loved.
